newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-SPD chief lists demands for German tax reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SPD chief lists demands for German tax reform.

text.p: German opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine on Friday spelled out his demands for tax reforms ahead of talks with the government next week, and welcomed new readiness to compromise shown by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

"At last!" Lafontaine told the Bild daily after Waigel said he would consider cuts in occupational insurance charges his Social Democrats (SPD) have sought. So-called labour overheads are the highest in Europe and are seen as a job-killer which has put 4.5 million Germans on the dole.

Cutting the labour overheads from July 1 is one of five demands Lafontaine said Chancellor Helmut Kohl must approve in a "a binding, fundamental decision" if face-to-face talks between the two next Tuesday are to succeed.

"German unification was financed above all through social security contributions by workers in both the east and the west," Lafontaine told Bild. "This unjust financing has cost hundreds of thousands of jobs."

Waigel's tax reform package, which would lower the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks ($17 billion), would begin next year and thus have no direct impact on Germany's ability to meet borrowing targets and qualify this year for European monetary union.
Any cut in social security charges this summer would most probably be revenue-neutral. Lafontaine said he favoured raising petrol taxes in an offsetting measure.
"We prefer an ecology tax reform. But we are also ready to look at the coalition's proposals," Lafontaine told Bild.
Waigel said on Thursday that reforms to the social security system and to pensions should be finalised first before contribution charges can be cut.
But he said a reduction of one percentage point in the charges could be possible if it is offset by an increase in indirect taxes.
The SPD's other demands are: the government must make it clear how much the tax reform will cost; entry-rate income tax must be cut; tax-free allowances and child benefits must rise.
Lafontaine's SPD walked out of earlier cross-party talks with the Kohl government in a row over coal subsidies.
And, accusing Waigel of leaving a gap of over 50 billion marks in his fiscal sums, the party refused to return to the negotiating table until Kohl agreed personally to take part.

Although there was little new of substance in Lafontaine's comments, it was clear that he was trying to build a more constructive atmosphere ahead of the make-or-break talks than has prevailed of late.

He did not directly oppose plans to cut top-rate income tax -- where the SPD has in the past opposed Waigel's plan to cut to 39 percent from 53. He instead linked the issue to his call for a child benefit increase.
"Kohl's planned cut in the top rate of income tax would cost 28 billion marks. An increase in child benefits by 30 marks would cost 3.6 billion marks," Lafontaine told Bild.
"It is better to help families than to make tax giveaways to the richest 10,000."

Waigel has said his package of cuts in income and corporate taxes would reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks -- but says the gap seen by the SPD would be closed thanks to the new investment and jobs arising from the reforms.

Coalition leaders have said they want tax legislation to pass the Bundestag lower house of parliament by the summer break. But they are hoping for a cross-party deal to defuse a possible parliamentary blockade by the SPD, which has a majority in the upper house.

SPD finance spokeswoman Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier rated the talks' chances of success at "50-50". She told ZDF television the SPD could go along with plans to cut corporate tax, but there was no reason for a big drop in top-rate income tax. ($ = 1.720 German Marks)
